messages.subject: R/qtl version 1.08-55
messages.body_plain:
A new version of R/qtl (1.08-55) has been released at its web site
(http://www.rqtl.org).  The Windows and Mac binaries should be
available within a few days.

See http://www.rqtl.org/STATUS.txt for a list of changes.  The major
changes are listed below; they are quite extensive.

We have added several new functions for exploring multiple QTL models.
The syntax for the fitqtl function has changed slightly, to give
consistency among various multiple-QTL functions

A document describing the use of the new functions is available at
http://www.rqtl.org/tutorials/new_multiqtl.pdf

We have done our best to test and debug the new code, but because of
the extensive changes, we fear that some bugs remain, so please view
results skeptically and let us know of any potential problems.

As always, I'd appreciate hearing any suggestions or comments or
complaints.

Karl Broman
kbr...@biostat.wisc.edu

------

Major changes:

  For all functions taking a "pheno.col" argument (including scanone
  and scantwo), this argument can now be a character string indicating
  the name of a phenotype. (Previously, it had to be a numeric index
  indicating the phenotype).

  fitqtl now takes a cross object and pheno.col (as with scanone,
  scantwo and scanqtl), rather than a column of phenotypes.

  Implemented Haley-Knott regression for the fit of multiple-QTL
  models in fitqtl and scanqtl.

  Added functions addint, addqtl, and addpair, for exploration of
  multiple QTL models.  addint tries adding all possible pairwise
  interactions, one at a time, to a multiple QTL model.  addqtl scans
  for an additional QTL to be added to a multiple QTL model.  addpair
  scans for an additional pair of QTL to be added to a multiple QTL
  model.

  Added functions addtoqtl, dropfromqtl, and replaceqtl, for
  manipulating a qtl object created by makeqtl().

  Added a function refineqtl(), for getting the maximum likelihood
  estimates of QTL positons (as best we can) in the context of a
  multiple-QTL model.  Added a function plotLodProfile which can
  create a figure with 1-dimensional LOD profiles for each QTL, in the
  context of a multiple QTL model, as is commonly created for multiple
  interval mapping.

  Added a function, tryallpositions(), for testing all possible
  positions for a given marker, keeping the order of all other markers
  fixed.

  Added a function, compareorder(), for comparing a given order of
  markers on a single chromosome to the current one contained within a
  cross object.

  Added some additional marker genotype codes for the phase-known
  4-way cross, for a dominant marker with both parents being
  heterozygous: 11 = not AC, 12 = not BC, 13 = not AD, 14 = not BD.

  Revised est.rf, for estimating recombination fractions between all
  pairs of markers, so that it can give results for many of the
  incompletely informative markers in a 4-way cross.

messages.subject: RIL and covariates/treatments
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am new to the group, R, R/qtl, and QTL analysis in general. I should
also state up front that I am a plant scientist. I have a multi-
location experiment with 2 treatments and I am trying to find
QTL*Treatment interactions. Is there a way to code my data such that I
am taking into account the nature of treatment.

As I understand animal studies, the treatments are applied to specific
individuals and those individuals are then genotyped with QTL analysis
completed on those genotypes. Simply put, one mouse/individual, one
treatment, one phenotype, one genotype. The coding becomes simple
because each individual is unique. Is this understanding correct?

For my population of RILs each "individual" is actually a line and a
sample of the line is grown with each treatment in several locations,
with replication. Currently, it has been recommended to me, and I have
seen in the literature, that the data is coded such that each trait
measured in each treatment, in each location, is considered a
different phenotype and analysed as such. But this is not exactly a
true representation of what is happening in the experiment. Would it
be valid to recode the data such that each treatment/location is
considered a different "individual", with the same genotype as the
same RIL in a different treatment/location?

This would potentially open the door to the use of covariates in our
QTL analysis. And potentially a better understanding of QTL*Env
interaction in plants?

Thanks for the help

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] RIL and covariates/treatments
messages.body_plain:
I've not spent any time thinking about this problem, and so there is no
code in R/qtl that explicitly deals with it.  In R/qtl, RIL data are
treated basically like a backcross, though taking account the map
expansion
in the treatment of missing QTL genotype information.  We allow a single
phenotype (e.g. the average) per line.

In the simplest situation, of a phenotype measured under each of two
treatments
for each line, I would be inclined to just work with the differences
(or the ratios), as a single measure.  Alternatively, I would work
with the
pair of measures, as a bivariate outcome, but there is no code in R/
qtl for
such multiple phenotype analysis.

I wouldn't want to artificially duplicate the individuals, with codes
indicating
treatment, but I don't have an alternative that could be accomplished
within
the scope of R/qtl.

Regards,
karl
-----------
Karl Broman
kbr...@biostat.wisc.edu
http://www.biostat.wisc.edu/~kbroman

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: RIL and covariates/treatments
messages.body_plain:
You shouldn't do this for the same reason that you should treat the
individuals
within RIL as independent.  I don't like to talk about valid or
invalid, but if
you phenotype 10 individuals from each of 30 RIL, and then analyzed
the data as
if these were 300 RIL  rather than work with the 30 averages), LOD
scores would
be inflated, and you couldn't do the usual sort of permutation test to
establish
significance.

If you were able to capture *all* QTL in one model, then the residuals
would
become independent, and it would be appropriate to work with all 300
individuals.
But if you can capture just a portion of the possible QTL, the
residuals will
be correlated, due to shared genotype the remaining QTL.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Error: cannot allocate vector of size 6.5 Mb
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Error: cannot allocate vector of size 6.5 Mb
messages.body_plain:
See the R/qtl FAQ (http://www.rqtl.org/faq):

4. I'm running out of memory; what should I do?
In Windows, by default you get 1 Gb memory (or the amount of RAM you
have on your computer, if that is less that 1 Gb). If you have 2 Gb
RAM, you need to use the command-line flag --max-mem-size to have
access to the additional memory.

Right-click on the R icon that you use to start R and select
"Properties". Then select the tab "Shortcut" and modify the "Target"
to include something like --max-mem-size=2G.

Alternatively, you can change the memory limit within R using the
memory.limit function, giving a new limit in Mb. (For example,
typememory.limit(2048) to change the memory limit to 2 Gb.)

See also the R for Windows FAQ and, within R, type ?Memory and ?
memory.size.

5. I'm still running out of memory; what should I do?
Of course, one is limited by the memory available on one's computer,
and so there are not many options.

First, clean up your workspace, removing objects that aren't important
to you. You can save objects to disk with the save command.

The multiple imputation method, as implemented, uses a particularly
large amount of memory. Consider using a small number of imputations
(n.draws) or a coarser grid (step) in sim.geno, or focusing on a
subset of the chromosomes.

karl

messages.subject: Permutation Testing
messages.body_plain:
I'm fairly new to QTL and would appreciate a confirmation that my
method is appropriate.

I'm looking for epistasis between markers in an eQTL study. I'm using
simple marker regression, examining each phenotype individually.

Since I'm looking for epistasis, I take the lod scores from the
twoscan output and subtract the lower-right (full) scores from the
upper-left (additive).

This score then gets compared with the permuted lod scores to
determine significance. The permutation testing returns 5 columns of
output... which one am I looking to compare with my original score for
epistasis? (is it the third column?)

Thanks for your help, Gregory Hannum, UCSD

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: Permutation Testing
messages.body_plain:
The (i,j) entry of the lod matrix from scantwo is:

   1-qtl LOD for position i (if i==j)
   additive LOD for pair (i,j) (if i < j)
   full LOD for the pair (i,j) (if i > j)

The locations for indices are indicated by the rows in the "map"
component of the output.

This is described in the help file for scantwo (see the section
"Value"):

"The first component is a matrix of dimension [tot.pos x tot.pos]; the
upper triangle contains the LOD scores for the additive model, and the
lower triangle contains the LOD scores for the full model. The
diagonal contains the results of scanone. The second component of the
output is a data.frame indicating the locations at which the two-QTL
LOD scores were calculated. "

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Re: Single Marker information from Effectscan
messages.body_plain:
Sorry; I'd thought about your question, but I forgot to respond to it.

You can get the estimated effects (and SEs) from effectscan if you
assign
the results to something; effectscan does return these effects, but this
is done "silently".

Consider the following:

   data(hyper)
   hyper <- sim.geno(hyper, step=2, n.draws=128)
   out <- effectscan(hyper, chr=4, get.se <http://get.se>=TRUE)
   out

karl

messages.subject: Permutation Testing query
messages.body_plain:
Hey,

I had a quick question regarding permutations.

Background:
My cross consists of 2956 genetic markers across 16 chromosomes. I'm
interested only the in the interaction effect between a pair of
markers. From the paper referenced in the man-file for "scan-two",
permutation testing is conducted by keeping an individual's genotype
constant while permuting its phenotype value.

Question:
(1) Is this how permutation is conducted in the function scantwo?
(2) Am I correct in assuming that the third column returned by a
scantwo with perms is the correct threshold to use?
(3) The LOD threshold located in the third column is described as "for
each pair of chromosomes we take the difference between the maximum
full LOD and the maximum additive LOD, and then maximize this across
chromosome pairs"; by each "chromosome pair" does this mean each
marker pair?
(4) Is the LOD-score threshold returned simply the maximum
"interaction" LOD score across all marker pairs for that particular
phenotype?

Thank you very much,
Rohith Srivas

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Permutation Testing query
messages.body_plain:
On Apr 28, 2008, at 5:15 PM, rsr...@gmail.com wrote:
> Background:
> My cross consists of 2956 genetic markers across 16 chromosomes. I'm
> interested only the in the interaction effect between a pair of
> markers. From the paper referenced in the man-file for "scan-two",
> permutation testing is conducted by keeping an individual's genotype
> constant while permuting its phenotype value.
>
> Question:
> (1) Is this how permutation is conducted in the function scantwo?

Yes, permutations with scantwo will permute phenotypes relative to
genotypes,
keeping the genotype data intact.

> (2) Am I correct in assuming that the third column returned by a
> scantwo with perms is the correct threshold to use?

The third column of the permutation results is for the epistasis LOD
score,
comparing the full two-locus model to the additive two-locus model.
I would go so far as to call it the "correct" threshold.  Different
people
have different views on the appropriate treatment of two-dimensional,
two-QTL
genome scans.

> (3) The LOD threshold located in the third column is described as "for
> each pair of chromosomes we take the difference between the maximum
> full LOD and the maximum additive LOD, and then maximize this across
> chromosome pairs"; by each "chromosome pair" does this mean each
> marker pair?

No we mean chromosome pairs.  We first maximize each of LOD[full] and
LOD[add've] across pairs of positions within a given pair of
chromosomes,
take the difference, and then maximize that difference across pairs of
chromosomes.

> (4) Is the LOD-score threshold returned simply the maximum
> "interaction" LOD score across all marker pairs for that particular
> phenotype?

It's nearly so, but see above.

karl
